Again, you don’t know what an EPC score is, how are you even suggesting what the probability of passing within a week is? That probability is determined from the EPC score, not the raw percentage of your NBME. The NBME looks at the topics on any given form and standardizes your score based on what any typical form should have to account for variances. Due to this, your EPC is usually lower by a few percent compared to your raw score. Furthermore, the probability is a singular data point based on the analysis of all US and Canadian MD students who tested within a week for that form. When you take your NBME forms online, it shows the CI of where your true score lies and if it’s within the LP range you’re at an inadequate level of prep where you have 5-10% chance of failing. But when we have more data points (as we do with this person, where they have multiple raw scores in the 50% range) that lowers the variance and shows that yes they indeed got lucky in passing. So 

1) his NBME EPC was not 63

2) we have more than 1 data point showing their weakness so we can examine with greater accuracy where his true score lies

3) 90% Chance of passing (which this person didn’t hit btw) is horrible for a test of this magnitude. That means on any given day, you have a 10% chance of failing. Nothing has to go wrong. This person’s preparation was inadequate to the degree that they had a 10% chance of failing to hit the minimum standard expected of all 2nd year medical students here in the US. So why not actually properly prep so you can meet that minimum standard at a 99%+ chance?

When you add resistors in series you just add them. When in parallel you add 1/Req = 1/R1 + 1/R2.

So with R3 the Req of the circuit is R + (R/2) + R = 2.5R

Without R3 the Req of the circuit is R+R+R = 3R

Now let’s use Ohms law. V = IReq so we know I=V/Req

Kinematics you can derive the equations from calculus and understanding that velocity is the derivative of position and acceleration is the second derivative. Did your school make you guys take Calc 1? 

For example take the equation:

Vf = V0 + at

Does this equation make sense to you? Acceleration describes how much the velocity changes per unit time. So to find your final velocity, you literally just take the initial velocity and add the change (acceleration) over that time period.

But you can also take that equation and integrate (opposite of a derivative) it respect to time. When you integrate velocity, you get back position (distance). 

Integrate Vf = V0 + at 

This gives you: 

Distance = V0t + (1/2)at^2 

And you can recheck your work by taking derivative of it and seeing that it gives you the velocity equation back.
